results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

The seven body units' summaries match p01-p07's controlling ideas in spec order (business model drives architecture; three pieces of knowledge; six chained questions and what follows; how to read the table; vocabulary and links to the book; Veldmark decisions per chapter; synthesis and start with marketplace-taxonomy). The five callouts are house format and match no spec paragraph.
Introduction callout 2 (WHY THE BUSINESS CARES): model and liquidity are presented as the two business facts the systems serve; a house-format callout, not a spec paragraph.
Introduction callout 4 (KEY POINTS): three bullets by design; the spec's basis says the KEY POINTS callout carries the part's claim in three bullets.
The Veldmark thread ¶2: synthesis plus where to begin is p07's single declared controlling idea (synthesis with its course-of-action takeaway and hand-off).

p01 states the thesis claim; p02-p04 support PI-1 (six questions in order, chapter to open per situation); p05 supports PI-2 (vocabulary later parts justify with); p06 shows that vocabulary becoming decisions (PI-2); p07 synthesizes. No orphan unit.
p01 example: the three marketplace kinds are followed in the same sentence by what they show (different identity, trust, payment and data systems even when search pages look alike).
Figure 1: the caption says what it shows (the business foundation every later system decision rests on).
Chapter table: the lead-in says each row gives a chapter's question and when to open it, which is what the table is for.

Veldmark scenario: framed by 'Using the part's vocabulary, chapter by chapter ... her team:' and followed by the synthesis; the reviewable-decision point is carried by the dated, approved/ratified decisions themselves.

p01->p02 (elaboration): 'Deciding what a group like Veldmark, with four of almost everything, should share takes three pieces of business knowledge' picks up the preface's group and elaborates the business-first claim.
p02->p03 (sequence): 'Six chapters ask these as six questions' carries the three pieces into the six questions in order.
p03->p04 (elaboration): 'Each row gives a chapter's question and when to open it.' picks up the announced table.
p04->p05 (cause_effect): 'This part supplies the vocabulary the rest of the book uses ... defined in that order by every chapter' turns the chapters into the vocabulary they leave behind.

p05->p06 (example): the lead-in reaches 'Using the part's vocabulary, chapter by chapter (not date order), her team:' after two scene-setting sentences; the example relationship is expressed within the lead-in.
p06->p07 (conclusion_summary): 'Together, the six chapters say what every later design must respect' summarizes the chapter-by-chapter decisions.
Hand-off: 'Begin with [[marketplace-taxonomy]], which asks where the marketplace's job ends.' carries the declared question to the next post.

results.quote: Deciding what a group like Veldmark, with four of almost everything, should share takes three pieces of business knowledge, supplied in order.
results.finding: Both readers name the organising principle the spec declares (large to small, chapters in prerequisite order) and mark no section unclear, but both lost the thread at the first mention of Veldmark: it is used as known and only identified in the last section ('Veldmark, the fictional marketplace group this book follows'), and 'four of almost everything' is not explained. The audience includes readers who arrive with one decision in hand, and the page itself identifies Veldmark, only too late; one clause at first mention fixes it.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 1: Veldmark appears as if the reader already knows it; the page only explains it in the last section; 'four of almost everything' is never explained.

results.quote: Six chapters ask these as six questions, each answer giving the next its vocabulary
results.finding: Both readers stopped on the conflict between 'each answer giving the next its vocabulary' and the later 'defined in that order by every chapter but the history one': if the history chapter defines no term, what does it hand to the capabilities chapter? The spec's how_why supplies the link (history shows why a systems inventory cannot be the unit for comparing brands, so capabilities are), but the draft never states it.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 2: the claim that each answer gives the next its vocabulary conflicts with 'defined in that order by every chapter but the history one'; unclear what vocabulary the history chapter hands on.

results.quote: Applies the share test per vertical: a shared-versus-specific table, ratified in April 2027, a month before the context map.
results.finding: Both readers stopped to re-sequence the dates: the bullets follow chapter order (bounded contexts before vertical requirements), so April is met after May, and the spec-prescribed remedy ('not date order' plus 'a month before the context map') draws attention to the inversion without explaining it. The difficulty comes from the spec's fixed bullet order combined with the scenario dates.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3: the dates make the jumps noticeable; 'a month before the context map' draws attention without explaining why the share test came first.

results.quote: Two more cases sit outside the five. The Poland overlap is a portfolio question.
results.finding: Both readers could not reconcile the two Poland mentions: the first bullet says the team 'resolves the Poland overlap', the fourth says it is 'a portfolio question' outside the capability overlaps. The spec only says the profiles bullet names the overlap; the verb 'resolves' is the draft's and creates the apparent conflict.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 4: the Poland overlap was described as resolved in the first bullet and comes back as a portfolio question; could not tell whether both describe the same decision.

results.quote: One duplicate is kept on purpose: Keybridge's software that sends agencies' listings to many property portals stays separate from Hearthly's intake of listings
results.finding: Both readers re-read this bullet because Keybridge and Hearthly appear here for the first time with no role, while Tradeyard and Motorvane are placed; the reader had to infer that Hearthly is the group's property portal. A short gloss on each name would remove the stumble.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 4: Keybridge and Hearthly are new names that appear only here, with no brand or country context.

results.quote: approved its €140 million Common Ground program in January 2027. Ingrid Halvorsen, Group Chief Architect since February 2027, spent her first months testing it against the business.
results.finding: Flow reader A (item 8) could not tell what Common Ground is, and the thread's purpose (testing the program against the business) depends on it. Reported by one reader only.

results.quote: Second, know how the industry got here: buyers go where sellers already are, so each country and category ended up with one leader; groups bought such leaders, and each brand still runs the systems of the industry wave it was built in, one of five from print columns to private-equity break-ups.
results.finding: Flow reader A (item 2) re-read the second item to find where it ended: it carries a whole causal chain and is much longer than the first and third items. Reported by one reader only.

Veldmark, its four brands, Common Ground, Ingrid and the failure patterns are on already_knows. Liquidity is glossed before use; marketplace profile and liquidity cell are glossed in KEY POINTS; capability, bounded context, vertical requirement profile and the share test are named and pointed to their chapters, as the spec's does_not_know entry allows. The flow readers' stumbles over Veldmark and the brands are recorded under flow_is_followable.
Opens on a direct, disputable claim with a concrete contrast; none of the weak patterns.
The conclusion applies the part's vocabulary in the declared Veldmark example, then synthesizes and hands off; it introduces no new subtopic and does not end on a bare restated thesis.

'Together, the six chapters say what every later design must respect before choosing a technology' is stated by no single section; the Veldmark list shows why it matters (dated decisions approved and ratified by a forum).
'which is why the book starts with the business' returns to p01's opening claim, and the last sentence sends the reader to the chapter that asks where the marketplace's job ends.

The intro reader predicts the declared roadmap: six chapters in order (model, liquidity, history, capabilities, boundaries, verticals), a table of when to open each, then the part's place in the book and Veldmark's decisions, with fitting evidence and tone. The AC-1 reader names all six chapters' subjects in order, matching the expected answer (including where the job ends, liquidity metrics, the waves, capabilities independent of systems, boundaries and the listing's master record, vertical differences and sharing).
Reader opens bounded-contexts for the listing-table meetings and vertical-requirements for the one-platform proposal, as expected.
Reader says the target must name the liquidity metric it protects, quotes the Veldmark rule, and says Part I's liquidity chapter supplies the metrics that later parts point back to, as expected.
